The Orange band surgeonfish Acanthurus olivaceus is a widespread acanthurid inhabiting Indo-Pacific coral reefs, where it undergoes a distinct pelagic larval phase before settling into benthic juvenile and adult habitats. The fertilised eggs are small and buoyant, measuring approximately 0.7 mm in diameter, and the resulting hatchlings emerge as yolk-sac larvae weighing just 0.00018 grams [Wwb = just 0.00018 grams] at birth. Following a period of endotrophic development, the onset of exogenous feeding occurs after the yolk sac is fully resorbed, marking a critical trophic switch. In benthic juveniles, growth proceeds steadily until individuals reach a total length at puberty of 11.55 centimeters [Lp = 11.55 centimeters], at which point gonadal recrudescence is initiated. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for fish of this size has been estimated at 68 grams [Wwp = 68 grams], reflecting the extensive somatic growth required before reproductive maturation can proceed. This length at maturity is modest compared to the ultimate total length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters] that large adults eventually attain under favorable reef conditions.

Life history studies conducted under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] have provided critical insight into the reproductive ecology of this surgeonfish. At this thermal regime, females spawn daily during the peak season, releasing one batch of pelagic eggs per spawning event, which translates to a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 1,808 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 1,808 eggs per year]. This high fecundity is characteristic of acanthurids that broadcast spawn into the water column, where egg and larval survival is subject to considerable stochastic mortality from predation and advection. The daily production of gametes demands substantial energetic investment, and gravid females are easily identified by their distended abdomens just prior to the spawning event. The reproductive output is closely tied to the thermal environment, and at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] the metabolic costs of gametogenesis are supported by the abundant algal resources available on the reef.

Adult Acanthurus olivaceus are iteroparous spawners that participate in mass spawning aggregations around the time of the new moon. A sexually mature adult in prime condition can reach a substantial ultimate wet weight of 2003 grams [Wwi = 2003 grams], making it one of the heavier-bodied members of its genus in the Indo-Pacific region. This large body mass supports a considerable gonadal investment and also allows the fish to defend feeding territories on the algal turf that constitutes its primary dietary resource. With respect to longevity, an exceptionally long-lived individual has been documented persisting in the wild for 35 years [am = 35 years], a remarkable lifespan for a fish of this size and one that underscores the relatively low natural mortality rates experienced by large acanthurids on protected reef systems at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. At the sustained water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] typical of tropical equatorial reefs, such extended survival is metabolically viable owing to the consistent availability of food resources throughout the year.

The pelagic larval phase of Acanthurus olivaceus is a critical period during which the tiny post-hatch larvae must locate suitable settlement habitat after a prolonged planktonic existence. The initial mass of each hatchling at emergence, a mere 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams] or 0.18 milligrams, is among the smallest recorded for acanthurids and reflects the high fecundity and low per-offspring investment typical of broadcast spawners. The transition from a pelagic teleost larva to a benthic juvenile involves a dramatic morphological transformation, culminating in the development of the characteristic orange band and the sharp caudal peduncle spines that define the adult. Once settled, the post-metamorphic juvenile begins a phase of rapid mass gain. The attainment of a total length of 11.55 centimeters [Lp = 11.55 centimeters] at puberty represents a size threshold remarkably consistent across several Acanthurus species, suggesting a phylogenetically conserved developmental trigger, with a corresponding wet weight of 68 grams [Wwp = 68 grams]. The gradual approach to the asymptotic length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters] typically spans several years, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the achievement of sexual maturity.

From a comparative life-history perspective, Acanthurus olivaceus exhibits a classic K-selected strategy among coral reef fishes, characterized by a large maximum body size and a relatively long lifespan of 35 years [am = 35 years] at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. When maintained at the tropical reef temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the daily reproductive rate translates into a substantial yearly output of roughly 1,800 fertilized ova per female [Ri = roughly 1,800 fertilized ova per female], which is released during daily spawning events. The ultimate wet weight of 2003 grams [Wwi = 2003 grams] achieved by the largest adults represents a more than ten-million-fold increase in body mass from the larval stage, a staggering growth trajectory supported by high ingestion rates of benthic algae. Collectively, these demographic parameters underscore the species' resilience to fishing pressure while also highlighting its dependence on intact reef habitats to sustain its full life cycle.
